Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: What is the difference between an AI “agent” and an ordinary chatbot? The word “agent” is everywhere in AI news, including in today’s item about ChatGPT. Is it just a new name for the same thing? The answer is at the end of this email.

  • AI from Anthropic and OpenAI publishes proofs of problems that have stood for half a century; a leading expert says “they are getting solved”. Just before Thanksgiving, AI from Anthropic and from OpenAI posted proofs of problems in the theory of computing that had stood for about fifty years. Anthropic’s internal Claude model proved that one classic calculation on a table of numbers (the “permanent”) is truly much harder than its near-twin (the “determinant”); OpenAI claims to have found the exact limit on how fast tables of numbers can ever be multiplied. The proofs are checked by computer, but Anthropic itself says no human mathematician has yet checked its proof. One expert calls it the result of the year; another warns that the most famous problem, P versus NP, is still far away. Read more and the background.
  • Physicists: AI now does the calculations that took us months, and students wonder what is left for them. A long report asks theoretical physicists what AI is doing to their field. One test made of unpublished research problems was beaten almost at once: OpenAI’s model solved 49 of 50, and found mistakes in some of the experts’ own answers. Leading physicists now thank AI in their papers, the number of new papers has jumped by about 30%, and one professor has stopped taking new students until he understands what their future will be. No major physics discovery has come from AI yet. Read more and the background.
  • Nvidia pauses server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries; Chinese AI companies’ new models slip. Nvidia has reportedly told its partners to pause shipments of AI servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia while it checks that American export rules are obeyed; data centres in such countries are estimated to supply about a quarter of China’s AI computing power. Reuters reports that two Chinese AI companies’ next big models are slipping by months as a result. Both reports are known to me only from short summaries. Read more and the background.
  • ChatGPT puts chatting and “work” under one allowance; some paying users will run out sooner. ChatGPT is merging its Chat mode and its Work mode, where it carries out longer jobs as an “agent”, into one window with one shared allowance; OpenAI says only its heaviest users should run out sooner. It also fixed a billing error, so the newest models will use up subscribers’ allowance 25–40% faster than last week. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: SAP reportedly plans to cut at least 10,000 jobs as it reorganises around AI, Expert: military attacks on data centres will not stop.

Answer to the question of the day. Not quite. An article in the Russian magazine Sistemny Blok puts it simply: a chatbot answers a question and waits for the next one; an agent takes a task and tries to finish it. Ask a chatbot for a flight to Rome next weekend under $300 and it gives you a list of links; the choosing, booking and writing it into your calendar are still your job. An agent can be given the whole errand: it compares flights, checks your calendar, books one, adds the trip and sends you the confirmation, and if the flight is sold out it looks for the next one without asking at every step. Inside, an agent is three things: a language model that does the reasoning, tools (search, a browser, your mail or calendar) that act as its hands, and a loop that lets it look at the result of each step and decide what to do next. Because an agent spends your money and changes things in the world, its mistakes cost more than a wrong answer, so people usually give it limits, such as “no purchase over $300”, and make it ask before paying. The article also lists the main risks: an agent can mistake a command hidden in an email or a web page for its owner’s instruction, and the more access it has to private data, the worse that can be. Its conclusion is a good checklist for anyone: before handing a job to an agent, ask how you will check the result, what it may do without asking, who is watching it, and whether its mistakes can be undone. (One of the connection standards the article describes, MCP, was created by Anthropic, the maker of Claude.) Sistemny Blok, “Jack of all trades: what an AI agent is” (article in Russian).
